content: Patients should not be made to wait for all program components to be fully implemented before receiving potentially life-saving interventions. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines emphasize the importance of patient support in ensuring good adherence to treatment and achieving improved outcomes. Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (TB) Treatment Regimens The treatment regimens for drug-resistant TB are defined by the duration of specific drug combinations, with variations noted for certain drugs. Examples of these regimens include: 1. Isoniazid-Resistant TB (Hr-TB): A 6-month regimen (6[H]REZ-Lfx) consisting of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin. Isoniazid may be added if a 4-drug fixed-dose combination (HREZ) is used. 2. Shorter Regimen for Multidrug-Resistant/Rifampicin-Resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB): A 9–11 month all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, and ethionamide for the first 4–6 months, followed by a continuation phase of 5 months with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. 3. Shorter Regimen for MDR/RR-TB with Fluoroquinolone Resistance: A 6–9 month regimen (BPaL) consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid. 4. Longer Regimen for MDR/RR-TB: An 18-month regimen with bedaquiline for the first 6 months, combined with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, linezolid, and clofazimine for the entire duration. Key Considerations for Treatment Isoniazid-Resistant TB (Hr-TB): Patients treated with the standard first-line regimen (2HREZ/4HR) face a higher risk of treatment failure, relapse, or acquiring additional resistance compared to those with drug-susceptible TB. Inadequate treatment of Hr-TB can lead to the development of MDR-TB, necessitating longer and more complex treatment with second-line agents. The recommended regimen for confirmed Hr-TB is 6(H)REZ-Lfx, provided rifampicin susceptibility is confirmed. MDR/RR-TB: In cases of fluoroquinolone resistance or extensive disease, individualized longer regimens are recommended. Operational Research and Monitoring: In settings with high resistance to other drugs in the regimen, modifications to the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen may be implemented under operational research. Diagnostic and Treatment Challenges Delayed Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST): Delays in DST results can complicate treatment decisions. For example, if isoniazid resistance is detected after starting a first-line regimen, rapid molecular testing for rifampicin resistance is necessary. If rifampicin resistance is excluded, the patient should be switched to the 6(H)REZ-Lfx regimen. Emergent Resistance: Unexpected resistance to one drug during treatment should prompt repeat DST for other agents in the regimen. Monitoring and Adverse Events: Regular bacteriological monitoring, including sputum smear microscopy and culture, is recommended to detect emergent resistance, especially to rifampicin. Liver and kidney function tests, as well as ECG monitoring, may be necessary based on clinical manifestations and medications used. Implementation and Programmatic Considerations Simplified Regimens: The recommended Hr-TB regimens do not have distinct intensive and continuation phases, simplifying treatment delivery and monitoring. Daily treatment is required, and intermittent regimens should be avoided. Cost and Accessibility: While the cost of the 6(H)REZ-Lfx regimen is higher than the standard first-line regimen, it remains affordable and feasible, even in low-income settings. Fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) and dispersible formulations are preferred for ease of administration, particularly in children. Data Collection and Reporting: Patients with Hr-TB should be registered in the TB register for monitoring treatment response and outcomes. Programs are encouraged to use electronic case-based databases to group patients by resistance patterns and share data for global reviews. Shorter All-Oral Bedaquiline-Containing Regimen for MDR/RR-TB A shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen (9–12 months) is recommended for eligible patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB who have not been exposed to second-line drugs for more than one month and have no fluoroquinolone resistance. This regimen has shown better efficacy and lower loss to follow-up compared to longer regimens with injectables. However, it requires careful patient selection and support to address challenges such as daily adherence, adverse drug reactions, and stigma. Conclusion The treatment of drug-resistant TB requires careful consideration of drug susceptibility, disease extent, and patient-specific factors. Adherence to WHO guidelines and the use of appropriate regimens can improve outcomes and reduce the burden of drug-resistant TB.
